Before agriculture we lived for millions of years off nature's bounty, as apex predators, in no danger of extinction. In only 12,000 years or so we've reached the brink of our own destruction, the environment that sustains us becomes more and more strained, our reach has surpassed our grasp, we have tools of destruction so powerful that our monkey brains can't comprehend them.

Better a small, stable society, than a massive, wildly unstable society right?

The evidence mounts that a cataclysmic event, a comet impact perhaps, brought humanity to the edge of extinction (edit: edge of extinction might be an exaggeration, but it was bad)right around the time of the agricultural revolution(http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/did-a-comet-hit-earth-12900-years-ago))[http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/did-a-comet-hit-earth-12900-years-ago/]. The remains of the first farmers tell the story of an incredibly harsh existence, a life of back-breaking labor. I theorize that mankind was initially forced to plow the fields as the only means to survive at the time, not because it was preferable to their previous way of life. There are stories of modern hunter/gatherers being taught farming, then when the teachers return years later they find the plots abandoned, the tribe having moved back into the jungle. One quoted saying something like "why work all day when there is food everywhere?"

When the Little Ice Age started to end, nature would have started to produce more, but agriculture is such a powerful weapon of ecological imperialism that it was now an unstoppable force. The farmers always needed more land, their population constantly growing, and they had the numbers and the technology to take it.

I heard an interesting theory the other day that the unspecified "forbidden fruit" of Genesis is actually wheat. A metaphor, blaming agriculture for Man and Woman being ejected from the Garden of Eden. An Apple would be a fitting metaphor in this context as well, considering how difficult it was to domesticate, another great triumph of agriculture.

I was just reading about pesticide problems on reddit, and it struck me, the utter perversion of trying to get 100% yield. So obsessed with complete domination that we're willing to poison our own food supply, and now the bees are dying. Oops.

edit: By "Some have argued" I'm specifically referring to Jared Diamond(Guns, Germs and Steel) and Daniel Quinn(Ishmael). Both great books. Very thought-provoking.

Some have argued that agricultural society is inherently flawed, a sort of "ecological imperialism" that is destined for collapse when it can longer expand. What do you think? Will technology save us?
